text: Washington, FBI headquarters on Pennsylvania Avenue. Director William Webster makes an announcement. The bureau has thwarted a plot to assassinate the prime minister of India, Rajiv Gandhi, on American soil during his visit with President Reagan. A few days earlier in New Orleans, FBI agents picked up a group of Sikh radicals right outside a hotel entrance. The man who led the FBI to them ran a war school in the Alabama Woods. The FBI said he saved Rajiv Gandhi's life. A year later, he'd be the one led away in handcuffs for plotting to blow up two cars. So whose side was he really on? You're about to see how a $350 course became an FBI trap, a terror headline, and a prison cell, and why two federal courts couldn't agree whether the plot was even a federal case. Before we get to whose side this man was on, let's hear how the FBI itself told the story that spring. It's a short version, and everything in it is right where it should be. On May 13th, 1985, FBI director William Webster said the bureau had thwarted a plot by Sikh radicals to kill Rajiv Gandhi during his visit to the United States. The court papers went bigger. The goal, they said, was the revolutionary overthrow of the government of India. And Webster added a line fit to be carved in granite. We won't allow our successes to blind us to the potential for terrorist activity in this country. To see why this was so serious, you need about 30 seconds of history. In the summer of 1984, the Indian Army stormed the Golden Temple in Umritzur, the holiest shrine of the Sikh faith, where armed separatists had dug in. Four months later, Indira Gandhi was shot dead by her own Sikh bodyguards. Her son Rajiv became prime minister. Sikh radicals wanted a state of their own in Punjab, and they considered his family enemy number one. Now look at it from Washington. In June 1985, Rajiv Gandhi is flying in to see Reagan on his first state visit. South Lawn, military band, dinner with the Reagan's. The administration wants to sell India technology and weapons, and, while it's at it, ease the country gently away from Moscow. Just that May, the two sides had signed off on the rules for transferring American technology. If the guest gets shot on American soil, all of that diplomacy goes into the ground with him. And the FBI saved it. A clean undercover operation, arrests before the visit, not a shot fired. It reads like a chapter out of a counterintelligence textbook. Only the press release left out one detail. Who came up with the whole thing? It wasn't the FBI that set the trap. The credit goes to a Vietnam veteran who ran a mercenary school in the Alabama Woods. He charged every student $350 for a two-week course. Stop and think about that for a second. In the mid-80s, right here in the United States, a school of war was operating out in the open. It advertised in a magazine and printed its price in the ad. You paid, you drove out to the woods, and for two weeks you learned to shoot live ammunition and fight like a commando. Like the karate classes my son took as a teenager. The veteran said all of it was perfectly legal. The Sikhs found the camp through that magazine ad. The owner turned his students over to the feds, and the feds walked in on a ready-made case. So the FBI didn't hunt anybody down. All that high-stakes geopolitics grew out of a strange little business that, by its owner's account, broke no laws. Keep that ad in mind. Before this story is over, the man who placed it will be called a hero, a businessman and a criminal, and every one of those labels will stick. And to get a sense of how big that business was, all you had to do was open one popular magazine. In the 80s, a certain kind of American man had his own magazine, Soldier of Fortune. At its peak, it sold around 150,000 copies, and the back pages carried the kind of ads you wouldn't find in your local paper. Tactical manuals, gear, and every now and then, an offer of services nobody asks about out loud. That's where the school from Alabama advertised, and it didn't hide what it was. It was called the Mercenary School. The owner's name was Frank Camper. In Vietnam, he'd served in long-range reconnaissance. Small teams that went out past the front lines and stayed in the jungle for days at a time. In 1980, he opened his school on the banks of the Warrior River in a wooded county outside Birmingham. Besides shooting, students learned to survive and to move through the woods without being found. The business model was smarter than it looked. Camper sold the same product twice, first to the students for $350, then to the government. By his own account, he'd started working for the FBI back in 1970. And information on the people who passed through his woods quietly made its way to the authorities. He described it without a shred of modesty. I invented it, I opened it. From that day forward, we were part of an intelligence operation. The arrangement ran quietly and kept everyone happy. Until late 1984. In the fall of 1984, a small group of Sikhs showed up in Alabama. Cecil Moses, who ran the FBI's Birmingham office, later put it plainly. They started shopping around for guns. And they showed an interest in mercenary training. According to Camper, during the course, they asked about time bombs and armored cars. Odd questions for a firing range in the woods. Camper told the authorities. Birmingham opened an undercover operation, and men looking for weapons needed someone to sell them weapons. That part went to an FBI agent named Thomas Norris. Thomas Norris was a former Navy SEAL. In the spring of 1972 in Vietnam, he and a single South Vietnamese partner made their way through enemy positions and brought out two downed American airmen. For that, he received the Medal of Honor. Six months later, a bullet hit him in the head. He lost an eye and part of his skull, and the Navy retired him for his wounds. In 1979, Norris walked into the FBI and asked them to overlook his disability. Director William Webster gave him this answer. If you can pass the same test as anybody else applying for this organization, I will waive your disabilities. Norris passed the same tests as everyone else. So picture it. A one-eyed Medal of Honor recipient, playing an arms dealer for men who'd trained at a mercenary school in Alabama. The curtain was up, and everyone in the room had a part to play. The lead actor's whole job was to get the customer to say too much. And the customers did. In early April, the group got to the real order. On their own initiative, they asked their new supplier to help arrange the assassination of Rajiv Gandhi during his upcoming visit to the States. And Gandhi wasn't the only target. They set it out loud to a federal agent. There was no reason to wait any longer. The FBI moved in. On May 4th, 1985, in New Orleans, agents arrested the plotters outside the hotel where another name on their list was staying, Bhujan Lal, the chief minister of the Indian state of Haryana. He'd come to America on a strictly private matter to see his eye doctor. Nine days later, William Webster, the same director who'd once waved a missing eye, announced the bureau's success. Clean work. Except that two names were missing from the list of arrests. The FBI had its headline. The question of whose side its star informant was really on would have to wait. And the man in Alabama who'd trained them was about to find out what legal is worth in a newspaper. Before that, though, the two who got away. Their names were Lal Singh and Aman Singh, and both lived in Queens. In New York, they were charged with conspiring against Gandhi, but nobody got to them in time. The FBI believed they'd slipped into Canada. On June 12, Rajiv Gandhi stood on the south lawn of the White House next to Reagan. The visit went off without a hitch. The FBI had defended its turf beautifully. On June 23, 1985, at Tokyo's Narita Airport, a suitcase exploded while baggage was being unloaded from a Canadian flight. Two baggage handlers were killed. Less than an hour later, Air India Flight 182 blew apart in midair off the coast of Ireland. 329 people died. It took the newspapers only a few days to put two and two together. Lal Singh was named a suspect in the bombing. According to Canada's Globe and Mail, 25-year-old Lal Singh had flown one leg of that chain of flights, and 33-year-old Aman Singh had been in Toronto just before the disaster. Indian officials added just one more detail. Lal Singh had trained at that very school in Alabama. In late July, India's foreign minister stood up in Parliament and demanded that the United States either shut down schools like that or outlaw them. It is unfortunate, he said, if the United States took an extreme legalistic view on the issue. Camper answered from Alabama, everything we do here is legal. I'm not responsible for them after they leave the school. And he added, we do not train terrorists. Camper called his business legal and considered the matter closed. Lal Singh's name would hang in the air for seven long years. Not until 1992 would a Canadian investigator find him in an Indian police station and sit down across the table from him. But first, the FBI's trap would end up under investigation itself. In May 1986, almost exactly a year after New Orleans, the authorities showed up at Camper's house in Huey Town. Only this time, they hadn't come for advice. The owner of the school was led away in handcuffs. The charges sounded like something written for a cheap TV movie. Two women from California, owners of private schools, wanted to get rid of some disgruntled former employees. According to the prosecution, Camper and two instructors from his camp helped them plan to bomb those people's cars. If you believe the prosecution, schools were ordering bombs from a school. In 1987, Camper was convicted on weapons and conspiracy charges and sentenced to 14 years. He called the whole thing a frame-up. He'd done too much for the government, he said, and now he was being taken off the board. Years later, a federal prosecutor in Los Angeles answered that in two sentences. He was not prosecuted because of any desire to silence him. He was prosecuted because of the crimes he committed. So whose side was Frank Camper on? The court locked him up as a criminal. But in 1988, while he was already behind bars, his work for the government was confirmed in public, before Congress. And Cecil Moses, that same FBI man from Birmingham, wrote a letter supporting his parole. A guy like Camper is a goldmine to law enforcement. A criminal to the court. A goldmine to the FBI. So whose side was he on? His own. I have no desire whatsoever to judge him. Picture a man who came home from the jungles of Vietnam with skills that hardly anyone needs in peacetime. Camper simply built his own world around them. The school on the Warrior River was neither a clever government trap nor an international incubator for terrorists. It was his own personal foxhole. He sold what he knew to anyone willing to pay, and he handed the information to the FBI, surviving the only way he knew how, with a perfect set of checks and balances between the radicals and the feds. The much-celebrated rescue of India's prime minister wasn't some calculated master plan. It was the natural result of that hard-edged balancing act. The veteran played by his own rules of survival, and he did what he set out to do. But once the headlines died down, the government stepped in. According to the case record, the New Orleans charges rested on a statute against conspiring to kill an official guest of the United States government. If he isn't an official guest, there's no federal crime, and he threw out the indictment. The government appealed, and a panel of the appeals court ruled the other way. In everyday life, a strong painkiller at the pharmacy takes a prescription with a doctor's signature. Two weeks of shooting live rounds in the Alabama woods took $350. That's it. A veteran who made his name on the art of survival and the trade in secrets ended up inventing a machine that just counts money. A life can't. Before you go, ever heard of Gringsit? Back in those days, Greenland walked out of Europe's common market just so it wouldn't have to share its cod. Next time, I'll tell you how the U.S. Army built a city under the Greenland ice. Until then, don't believe every press release.
